To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the silicon microstrip detectors used by Fermilab experiment 771 were damaged by radiation and that the use of a fast amplifier contributed to the damage.

(1) the pulse height from the amplifiers began to decrease at a fluence near 2 × 10 p/cm2, (2) the signal was lost completely at a fluence around 6 × 10 p / cm 2, (3) the signal loss was due primarily to the fast amplifiers, and (4) the signal loss is not due to the depletion of charge from the silicon bulk.
the mean pulse heights from our silicon microstrip detector fell to zero at a fluence near 6 × 10^13 p/cm2.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the silicon microstrip detectors used in FermilAb experiment E771 were not seriously damaged by the radiation environment of our experiment.

we were able to measure the mean pulse height of the detector to within 5% of its pre-irradiation value up to a fluence of 2 × 10 13 p/cm2, and that the signal-to-noise ratio of our detector remained above 5:1 at this fluence.
we were able to obtain good data for a fluence of 2 × 10 13 p/cm2, but that we were not able to operate the detector in the 10 14 range without a significant loss in signal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the silicon detectors used in E771 were not designed to operate in a high radiation environment.

the silicon microstrip detectors used in experiment E771 were able to operate at high bias voltages for fluences of 9.3 × 1013 and 1.2 × 1014 p/cm2, respectively, without significant degradation of their performance.

we can expect the performance of the silicon microstrips used in E771 to degrade by approximately a factor of two in the next 10 years of running at the Fermilab Main Injector, which is a much smaller degradation than that seen in the E771 detector.
